THE SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION

Jazz Oral History Project
Interview with Jimmy Maxwell
Reel 1

Conducted by Milt Hinton
April 16, 1979

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
AREA CODE 202 347-5395

This is March 20th, Tuesday night, March 20th, 1979. And I'm sitting here talking to James -- what's your middle name, James?
Kendrick.
James Kendrick Maxwell.
My father's first name.

Is that so? Well, Jim, we just want to rap with you a little bit about some of the things, your good times and your bad times. And what you've done and who you are, from when you came, that sort of thing. So now that we've established the date you just go on and tell us about your birth and your family and whatnot.

Well, I was born in Stockton, California although my family lived in Tracy. This is in the San Joaquin Valley in California. It was 1917*and the area then was semi-desert. There was no irrigation or anything at that time and it was very desolate. But it was beautiful countryside. I appreciated it more after I left. And as a child, we were three or four miles from the nearest neighbor so I played mostly with animals. Had a pet snake, pet chicken, pet dog, cat and things of that kind.
However, we had a big family. We lived with my grandfather and my great grandfather, two or three uncles and cousins, so there was always a lot of people around. And my great
*January 9, 1917.
grandfather had fought in the Civil War and was found of telling about the time he'd seen Lincoln.
What was his name, James?

Well, his name was Reid (PHONETIC), too. See, my grandfather's name was Gilmore Reid and I'm trying to think of my great grandfather's first name. I really can't think of it at the moment. And they came from -- my mother's side, this was my grandfather Reid, great grandfather Reid was Scotch Irish and his wife was, I believe, German Jewish. And on my mother's mother's side her father was Scotch Irish, he was from New Orleans and he was an artist there and when the Civil War started he went up to New York to join the Northern army.
What was your mother's name?

My mother's name was Margaret Mary Reid. And this great grandfather said he was married to what was called a Creole woman, which means she was French, Spanish, Indian -- I don't know what. But judging from the pictures she was dark, some kind, which was probably the reason he went to the North when the Civil War started.
(Laughter.)

I have pictures of them. So we -- there was no electricity in those days so no radio or anything. In the evenings people sat around and sang songs. Everybody played musical instruments. So from as far back as I can remember,
I've heard music.
What kind of instruments would they play?

Well, mostly violin, banjos, mandolins, guitars and when I was four my grandfather Maxwell, my father's father, gave me a cor-net. One of my uncles played cor-net and one played baritone horn. But they played mostly old Scotch-Irish songs or they played country music. My grandfather played country fiddle. He held it down on his stomach and played on his stomach, like a bass viol. And my mother played violin, but she had gone to Conservatory. She was a good violinist. So we all sat around and played in the evening, by ear, everything.
Were there any brothers or sisters? You mentioned it was a large family.

Well, it was but I had a brother who died in 1919 in a flu epidemic. And then I had a sister born in 1920, Marjorie, who is still alive. Then there was no children until 1932, I had another sister, which was born in 1932 and she died last year, 1978. My sister Marjorie is still alive.
But none of them -- Marjorie tinkled around the piano but none of them were very interested in music. My father was a very good clarinetist. He told me he was known as the Boy Wonder in the Navy.
Oh, he was in the Navy?
He ran away from home in the 6th grade and joined the Navy. He was very big for his age. And maybe he was very old for the 6th grade, too. I don't know.
What kinds of schools were around there, Jimmy? You grew up on kind of like a farm?

Well, they had one classroom. My grandmother was one of the teachers and everybody from the 1st to the 8th grade was out in the country school. But by the time I started school they decided -- I went into the town school. I had to walk into town three miles to get to the school every morning and it used to be bitter cold, to carry this cornet in every morning. I was four years old, that means I've been carrying a cornet or trumpet every day of my life for 58 years. So that's why one shoulder slopes a little more than the other.

But I was told that when I was young my mother gave me a half-size violin, but I don't remember it. She says the reason I don't is I took it out in the irrigation canal and stuck the bow the in the F hole and put a handkerchief on it and sailed it down the canal. I never liked violin as a boy. Said it sounded like a woman crying.
What was this canal in your neighborhood?
Well, they were putting in irrigation ditches then to irrigate. They started growing alfalfa and

things. Now it's big wine country. They have grapevines and orchard country. But at that time, as I say, it was all desert. And my grandfather, as a matter of fact, was what they called a mule skinner. They had a team of mules and a scoop that does the work of a bulldozer. And he helped build some of these canals and roads.
A scoop? What is that, like a plow or something?

Well, it's like the scoop on the front of a bulldozer except it was pulled by mules. And that's why they called them mule skinners, the people that ran them. And when I was a boy it used to be interesting for me. I would go out with him and they would unearth Indian artifacts, even sometimes skulls or bows and arrowheads. Things of that kind.
That's very interesting. There must have been a lot of Indian artifacts like that around, I guess.
Well, there were. There were not many Indians left in that area. Well, there were many descendants but they really had become Americanized. They were no longer Indians.
When did you get into any school bands, anything like that?
Well, I went to school when I was four years old to go to kindergarten. They said I was too big so they put me in the first grade. So I was eligible to play in

the school orchestra. I remember they taught me the fingering then. And I played all through school on this cornet my grandfather had in the Spanish-American War, a Büscher cornet. And I was never too gung-ho about it. I never practiced particularly, other than just playing with the family. Because most of my early life I wanted to be a priest, especially from the time my brother died. I wanted to see God and I felt I wanted to be a priest. So I was very religious and it wasn't until I got to high school and went to seminary I realized I wasn't going to be a priest that I realized I was probably going to be a musician. Because I never studied. But I listened to Louis Armstrong records and Duke Ellington records all day and practiced all night. Ditched classes to go back in the auditorium and practice.
What made you decide you wanted to be a priest? Did they have priests around -- anybody in you community?

Well, I think a very materialistic reason. The catechism taught we were put on this earth in preparation for eternity. And I thought the best thing to do was get in on the ground floor and be a priest.
Hey, that's pretty good.
Truthfully, that was part of my reason. But basically, I was very interested in God and I was very angry when God took my brother, as I was told, that nobody
woke me up to see God. I think I spent the rest of my life trying to see him. Truthfully, this is not a joke. I'm saying it in a laughing way but I'm serious.
You mentioned, and just for the record, when you went to kindergarten you were too big. And just as a matter of record, you must have always been big. How tall are you now?

Well, I'm 6'4" now. In the 8th grade I was 6' and my feet were size 12. It was very embarrassing. I felt awkward. But I went to a Catholic military school in the 9th grade and they made me stand up straight and march and everything. So I didn't get a stoop or anything.
So how long did you stay in California? What was your school life and all like?

Well, I did very well in school if I liked the subject. If I didn't like it I practically failed it. I think if my grandmother had not been a teacher I wouldn't have gotten through. They did it out of consideration for her. I would get A-- in high school, I would get A's in chemistry, biology, art and music. I would fail in things like English or history or political science. But I didn't know -- nobody'd ever told me that you're supposed to take the book home and study it. I just thought if you didn't learn it when they told it to you, that's too bad. So I could remember anything on a subject I liked.

My children saw my report cards when they were in high school and they were looking at me in amazement saying, 'How do you get an F in gym?' It was simple, I refused to go out for football the first year and they flunked me. So the next year I went out for football.

That's quite interesting and difficult to understand, knowing you as being respected as one of the most learned of musicians that speaks many, many languages, more than one, especially. And we know about all of your great technique, great first trumpet player and all these things. But it was just a matter of what you liked, huh?

Yes, I've always read an awful lot. When I was in school I think I read every book in the public library. And I read every book in the Encyclopedia Britannica. I liked to read books. I like to read encyclopedias and dictionaries, miscellaneous information. I don't remember much of it but I just -- it's just interesting to me to read facts about different things.

But most everything that I have learned I taught myself, with the exception of Japanese. I went to Columbia University and studied that. And actually, I was very surprised, I got an offer from the FBI for a job. I had gotten a very good record, the highest record there in Japanese for four years. So they automatically send in names of people with language aptitudes.
I want to get into that a little later on, more about your languages. But if we can get back to your early days, getting into trumpet playing and first bands, and that kind of thing.

Well, we had a good school band. We used to go to the contests, the county and state contests, and always win in our category. We had a very good teacher in grammar school. Then when I went to military school in high school we had a very good marching band there. We had a teacher there from the San Francisco Symphony who -- he played English horn himself but he was an old Italian gentleman and very inspiring man. He loved music and he got me to like it. He used to stay up late at night and play duets with me. And more or less taught me most of the music that I knew, as far as formal training goes.

And while I was there I won the medal for music in military school. Then when I was -- see, in 1932 I started to work on the trumpet. While we were in school we had a little group and we played and somebody told me, you know, don't just play the melody, you have to play a little jazz and ad lib. And I said, well, what's that? And he said, did you ever hear Louis Armstrong, and I said, yes. He said, well, like he does. And I said, you know, that's what I'm trying to do.
And they explained to me you'd have to copy the records at first, you know, until you got the feeling for it. And then
later you'd find little by little your own ideas would start coming in.

So when I first started to play I copied his solos note for note. And I would copy anybody's solos; but I did not ever like Red Nichols or Bix Beiderbecke very much. And when I went later years -- well, I'll get into that, it became kind of an issue. It was very racially divided in California, musicians were.
Do you recollect that old Italian teacher's name? Just for the record, who taught you to play French horn and --

English horn he played, like an oboe. Oh, I have a terrible memory for names. I had an accident a year ago and shook my head up a little bit and it's gotten worse, my memory for names. Salvatore -- naturally.
(Laughter.)
You want to tell us about California, how things were?

Well, I started playing for dances in a place that was a bootleg place. This was during Prohibition and they sold drinks and they had lady entertainers there. There's another name for that kind of place, too.
(Laughter.)
And they paid $2.00 a night, which was not great money in those days but the average working man made $30.00

a week for a 60 hour week, 10 hours a day, 6 days a week. So that wasn't -- proportionately it wasn't too bad. And of course I enjoyed it very much, just playing. I don't know how good the musicians were I played with. I remember the piano player was generally -- he was generally pretty foggy. He was drunk or something. And I know that's where I had my first drink, in that place. Somebody gave me some gin and I thought they had pulled a joke on me and given me some aftershave lotion. I got very sick from it.

So that was 1932 that I first started working. And I was still in high school then. And I would work on the weekends. Fortunately, my mother and father didn't know where I was working so they didn't stop me. My father was very fond of gambling so that means he was always a little short of money. So he was perfectly happy that I was making some money because sometimes he'd wait up for me and he would say -- he wouldn't take it from me. We'd play a few friendly games of cards and then he would take the money.
(Laughter.)
It wasn't necessary. I would have given it to him gladly but he felt the honorable way to do it was to take it from me, cheating me in cards.
It was difficult, living in the San Joaquin Valley. The other kids in town were interested in music but not to the extent I was. And not having any money, this is the Depression

years, my father was out of work for several of those years. There wasn't that much jazz coming out to California anyhow. As Wingy Manone once said, it never got over the Rocky Mountains. But about once a month one Armstrong record would come out and one Duke Ellington record would come out. And some way I would beg, borrow or even steal, truthfully, for one of these records. And I started copying off -- also tried to copy off the Duke Ellington records.

I didn't know anything about harmony or anything but I knew the names of triads. So if I had what I guess you would call a C ninth, that -- a C 13th. I remember "Blue Ramble" is the first tune I copied and the chord -- and I had a C, A, E, G, D, B flat, see, in the bass. So I called that a G minor chord and A minor chord with C in the bass.

Now, years later I was copying off some of those records for Mercer Ellington because they had lost the arrangements in the band. And I was telling him when I was young how I'd written chord symbols, I didn't know how to write them. I said, I'd write A minor, G minor with C in the bass. And he kind of laughed and I said, what's funny. He said, that's what Poppa did.
(Laughter.)
And he explained that Duke wrote everything in triads, which was interesting. Because when I copied the records, I could follow each part. And I would hear the three trumpets

going C, A, E down. But above the third trumpet would be the trombone playing in G. And I couldn't figure out why he was doing that. And after Mercer explained to me that he wanted a perfect triad of an A-minor in the trumpets and a G-minor in the trombones, that's how the G got over the third trumpet. And that clarified a lot of copying arrangements later, when I couldn't be sure what I was hearing. If I followed that principle, it would come out right. Because Duke had told -- he said that he wanted every section to sound good by itself so that he had no rubs, you know, people playing half-steps apart or full steps apart.

So the first record I copied was "Blue Ramble." And it must have taken me six months to copy that thing and I couldn't get anybody to play it anyhow. You know, the kids in high school sort of -- they weren't that interested in playing.

The first ARmstrong record I ever copied was "When You're Smiling," which goes up to a high E on the trumpet. In those days if the trumpet player could play up to a high C they thought it was pretty phenomenal. So it was kind of lucky for me that I listened to Louis Armstrong. I didn't know that the trumpet was supposed to stop at C so when I was in high school I could play up to high G. Because it's a matter of your attitude, how high you play, basically. You know, just as young guys come along now, they think in terms of double high C. Well, I don't think that high so any notes above G, I can't
tell you what they are if I hear them. But, you know, the younger players, many of them think high. They listen to Cat Anderson, Maynard Ferguson.

I was just wondering, that was pretty advanced to be able to copy. Most youngsters couldn't copy those things. You must have had an extremely good ear and a lot of patience to keep playing this record over again.

Well, I'm very stubborn. And I would sit -- it was the summertime. I spent the whole summer just trying to copy this three minutes of music. And maybe four or five hours a day. And it would just take each instrument one note at a time and write them down. And I'd go back over it and try to figure out the rhythmic pattern. And that was what gave me the most trouble.

It gave me the most trouble on Louis Armstrong solos, trying to write those out, until it dawned on me that when he played he thought in eight. And if you write it out as in double time, then it's perfectly clear. But when I was young I tried to write them out in eighths, I'd say, "rush" or "slow down" instead of writing the 16ths in there that I should have written.
Pretty interesting.
Well, I don't know how interesting it is.
Well, it took a lot of really inventiveness to do that. And what was your first band you

started to travel with? What did you get, around California? Well, the first band I went out of town with was Gil Evans in 1933. A local friend of mine played in this great band. We all heard about the Briggs-Evans band up in Stockton. Ned Briggs was a bass player, Gil Evans was a piano player. And they all copied arrangements off from Casa Loma and Isham Jones and people like that. And they needed a trumpet player and I went up and tried out. And I almost didn't get the job because I always had trouble reading whole notes. I always wanted to play them twice as fast. But I got the job eventually.

So I stayed with them and I copied off a few arrangements for them. I copied off some Ellington arrangements, some Lunceford arrangements and an Earl Hines arrangement, I liked "Rosetta," which I insisted on singing.
(Laughter.)
: Oh, you got into that? Always had that music around the house as a kid.

So that was the first band. The day after I graduated high school in 1934, we went up to Lake Tahoe and that was our first out of town job. We would go out of town for one night, maybe. But there would be some of these schemes, you'd give a promoter $50.00 and he would give you a booking up in the Sierra Nevada Mountains. And we'd ride all day long in the back of a truck and get up there about 7:00
o'clock and find this old, broken down building and nobody around. And find out we'd been clipped for $50.00. So we'd drive back.
There were some questionable experiences we all had.

Yeah, I know everyone went through those things. But the job up at Lake Tahoe was a nice job. It was Globben's (PHONETIC) Chalet and it was a place built out over the lake. And the lake had not become polluted. You'd dive in and drink water. And that summer Max Baer was up there training for his second fight with Carnera. We had to sit around at night and watch them show movies of his first fight. And he couldn't get a sparring partner and I guess you can guess what I'm leading up to, because at that time I was 6'4". And he wanted somebody Carnera's size and I said, oh, no. And he said, well, now you can wear a mask and I promise I won't hit you hard. I'm just trying to get somebody to aim at. And I said nothing doing. And I said, what if I give you a lucky punch, you know, and you forget yourself and really hit me? I won't play again. No, he said, I'd never do that. So two or three times I did, I sparred with him two or three times a week.
That's really interesting. That was Lake Tahoe. That's a magnificent piece of water up there.
Yeah, that was beautiful there. And
the lake used to be like bluing, you know. You couldn't see the bottom. It was pure but it was so deep. At that time there was a myth that you couldn't find the bottom.
I've heard that, too.

I should go back, maybe to -- I talked about my mother's side of the family. My father's side of the family also all played music instruments and they were itinerant workers. They used to go up and down the West Coast, mostly fruit picking. And just get enough money ahead to buy tobacco and food and make some home brew. And they all lived in tents. And we could wake up someday and there'd be three or four tents pitched out next to the house on the empty lot and a fire going. You know, people were more easy-going then. The police would hit them today. But they'd be camped out there and they'd sit around at night and they'd all play guitars and I guess they sang the music. I don't know too much about it but they call it bluegrass music now. And that's the kind of songs they used to sing.

My grandmother used to be an organist in the Baptist church and she knew lots of hymns. Carried this harmonium around and she'd play like a rock and roll bass (humming) and they'd all sit around and sing gospel songs. I think I had a better time with them because they used to get pretty worked up and shoot off pistols in the air.
Had more rhythm.

Yeah. My mother's family is Puritan, my father's family were swingers. My father, oddly enough, never drank. The rest of his family made up for him. And so everybody seemed to play some instrument in my family. I guess it's natural that I just sort of drifted into it. But I realized one day, with Gil Evans' band when we went down to southern California, I was never going to be a priest, I wasn't going to be a doctor. This was really what I wanted to do because this is what I spent my whole time doing, anyhow.
That's the Gil Evans we know?

Yeah. After we came back from Tahoe we tried to get a job in Sacramento and we hung around there for a couple weeks. The union wouldn't let us work the club and when you go without food for four or five days it gets a little rough. And we'd all try to think of girls we knew in Sacramento and get invited over to dinner or something and say, well, how about bringing my friends.

So that didn't work out. So we went back to Stockton. We worked in a place called the Dreamland Ballroom and I went back to junior college in Modesto and I used to hitchhike up to Stockton every night and play all night and then hitchhike back in the morning and go to school. And while we were there, lots of the road bands would come through, the Gene Coy and Merle Carlson. Do you remember that band?
I remember the name. What's the

other one you said? Merle Carlson. That was a white band. Gene Coy was a black band, though. And they had some good players. They had a hell of a good trumpet player in that band I liked very much. And it was -- you know how times were then. When they couldn't get jobs playing they would be a baseball team. Softball was very popular then and they were sort of the Harlem Globetrotters of softball. And they'd take on any of the local teams, I guess for $25.00 or something.
I'm glad you mentioned that. Elaborate on that a little bit because nobody's mentioned that yet and that's sure a happening.

Oh, yeah. You know, actually I have a recollection of the Mills Brothers coming through when they were down on their luck and they stopped in our high school and said, you know, $50.00 to get us to San Francisco, we'll give a concert to the kids. This was in 1932.

Now I asked -- later I worked with them a lot and became friendly with them and I think Harry's the one I asked about it. Of course, he wouldn't remember it. He said he doesn't remember Tracy, particularly, but he said, we did that plenty of times.
Who'd you ask?
One of the Mills Brothers. Harry, I think. And I was telling him when I was a kid, I said, I've

got the strongest recollection that your group stopped in my high school. And I said, you know, you were famous then because I'd heard records of you. I said, was that a possibility? He said, yes, sometimes we'd get down on our luck. Had a record but, you know, in those days the artists didn't get all the money off that record. And they'd get stranded someplace and stop in a school or someplace and give a concert.

But some of these road bands like Gene Coy -- there was another one, they would just work their way around the different towns without much advance notice, you know. They'd pile into a couple of cars. Well, the same way Gil's band traveled. We had an enormous old Cadillac and get 10 musicians in that car and a trailer for the instruments. That's how we traveled, some of these old bands would travel. Or they'd get an old, broken down school bus.
I went through all of that, Jimmy. With my bass on the side, on the mud guard on the side of the car.

I know. After I left Gil's band I worked out in the Middle West with a band like that. We'd play up in Montana and Idaho. And we'd go in these blizzards where everybody would have to take off their overcoat and we'd strap it over the hood of the car so the motor wouldn't freeze. And you had to leave the window open for the driver to look out. So one guy'd wear a coat and sit on the radiator hood with a
flashlight so they could see the white line down the middle of the road and pilot, you know.
So, you know, all the bands went through things like that in some of those days.

Sure did. That road traveling was kind of rough. You know, I remember Cab Calloway's band, years later when things got to be good, he'd still organize little basketball teams, you know. Or football or baseball teams. And I guess this was an outgrowth of those times when a band hit town and there was no gig. You just organized as a baseball team and play the local guys.

Well, that's the way it worked with those bands. I remember, you know, bands being down on their luck. This was after I'd gone down to Los Angeles about 1936 or '37. I saw four or five familiar faces standing around the street in Tracy one day and one of them said, aren't you Buck Clayton? And he said, yeah. He said, what are you doing here? He said, I'm here with my band and the promoters run out. No money and everything so they had Buck Clayton, Lee Young and about six of the others. They said they hadn't eaten for a couple days so I took them home to my house and my mother gave them all dinner.
The bands would travel. They'd just go up the coast and come down and say, look, you know, you've got a hall. We'll put on a dance for a certain percentage.

Surely. I can remember around Chicago, we had quite a few places to play, naturally, in Chicago. But the younger guys like myself at that time, you know, early thirties, the younger guys like us couldn't get a job in town. And we used to get in the car and go out to what they called roadhouses. That's the little saloon out on the highway, we'd just unpack and go in and start playing. If people would give us a couple bucks, we stayed.
That's what we did, too, yeah.
If they didn't give us anything, we'd go down the road to the next place.

That's what I did. Or I would go out by myself. I didn't have a car but if I could get a friend to take me out to one of these roadhouses or just out to one of the country dances, I would go in if they had arrangements or if they didn't have arrangements I'd say, look, let me sit in and play solos. I'll play for nothing, couple of beers or something, just -- I remember doing that many times.
(Break)

You were talking about those guys--Buck Lee Young out on the road and you took them home. It wasn't too chic, bringing black cats home with you in those days. I know we had a kind of tough time sometimes.
Oh, yeah. Well, the town I came from was basically a Southern town. It was mostly Anglo-Saxon Protestants from Texas, Oklahoma, Arkansas and that area,

Mississippi. And Catholics were not very popular, either. We were Catholics. And it wasn't too much of a problem with black people because there weren't that many black families in Tracy. But they took out their venom on the Mexicans, the Japanese farmers and the Catholic families.

My father worked on the railroad and he once found a list in one of the cabooses of members of the Ku Klux Klan and he turned it into the division headquarters thinking he would get the guys to lay off, a man named Sullivan. Unfortunately, Sullivan was a North Irishman, a Protestant and a member of the Klan and they burned a cross in our yard a couple of weeks later.
They burned a cross in your yard?

Yes, and it was pretty frightening. I was very young then and my father had to carry a revolver to work the next couple of years. Most of their hosility was toward Japanese farmers and Mexican farmworkers. There weren't that many black people in town, maybe one or two families. And actually, going back to the place I first played in was -- can I use all the words?
Sure, absolutely.

A whorehouse down what they call south of the tracks. This was where Mexican families lived and the non-Anglo-Saxon families lived, on the south side. And this one street, I'm embarrassed to tell you the title, was called

King Nigger Alley.
(Laughter.)
And that's where the black prostitutes were and the classier ones lived down at the end of the street. Frieda Price had this house with a lot of girls where I played. And my father, as I told you earlier, was a gambler. And although he was born in Texas and raised in Missouri, he didn't give a damn what anybody was as long as they were gamblers. So he would often bring some guy down on his luck over to the house, he would be a black guy. If he was a bigtime gambler, he liked him.

One of my earliest recollections, when I was about four we lived two miles out of town and for some reason they were running this black guy out of town. In those days they literally ran you out of town. The sheriff sat on the fender with a shotgun and this poor black guy is running in front of the car. Now, if he runs off the road they shoot him and if he doesn't keep running, they run over him.

My father saw them and he had a violent temper. He ran out and pulled the sheriff off the car, hit him on the head with a shotgun and threw him back in the car and chased them off and took the black guy into the house, you know, washed him up and fed him. So we had to keep the house locked again for another couple days.
So I do know a little bit about prejudice but I know

I myself used the word "nigger," not knowing that was a bad term until years later. I had a friend, Lloyd Reese, and one day he said, "You know, Jim, I know how you think, but please don't use that word anymore." I said, "What's wrong with it?" He said, "That's not a good word." I said, "What do you mean it's not a good word? What should I say?" He said, "Well, call us Negroes or even call us Oxford Grays, but don't call us niggers." And I wanted to die, you know. I sank into the ground. So then I spent the next month thinking how many times I'd used that word to the wrong people.

In junior college I had this black guy I used to wrestle with and box. And I did know about prejudice because I was a little surprised at junior college, he was sort of in with this bunch of guys, musicians and sort of like a hep crowd there that I was with, being a musician. And we would all go to the dances together and I remember we would dance with his girlfriend and he would dance with white girls and I do remember I was surprised. So I did know a little about prejudice.

And I also remember, once we were wrestling or something and he hurt me and I called him a black bastard. Now, when I said a black bastard, it didn't mean race. Like they say a black Irishman, that's an Irishman that's lost his faith. And a black bastard was another guy that was a dirty bastard. It had nothing to do with his race but as I saw this look in

his eyes it dawned on me, this guy is black. And I thought he was going to kill me. I didn't know whether I was frightened or heartbroken. I started to cry and apologize because I knew I'd hurt his feelings.

But there was this thing about it. I know I was kidded in my hometown because my neighbors would say, "Well, you're never going to be happy until you have a green suit and play with a nigger band, or something." And I said, that's right, you know. Or guys would kid me, I'd see a black girl and say she was pretty, or something. And they'd say, "Man, you think like a nigger" or something, you know.

But I'll be very truthful, I always felt kind of flattered. When I realized all my favorite musicians were black and I had the feeling in those days that black people had an edge on jazz. And in all honesty, I still think so. Now, whether it's a matter of race or culture or whatever, it's not important, that means nothing.
It's cultural or something.

I think so, too. Because you see little kids, white, black, any other color, and they can keep time and everything. But in our culture you get inhibited and tied down and you don't hear that kind of music.
In that kind of environment it turns out that way. I think that Zoot(Sims) is about as black as anybody I know.
Yeah, I guess so. Because, you know, it's more comfortable for me to think it's cultural because if it's inherited, I don't have a chance. But there was this undercurrent.

Now, when I went to Hollywood, they had all these places, these clubs, guys used to go around to different clubs and sit in and play. Now, many times -- many times, maybe four or five times, I would get the comment, look, if you want to play like a nigger, you can't play here. Why don't you go down to Central Avenue? Well, they didn't particularly want me at Central Avenue, either, because they had plenty of good players of their own. But that was the kind of stuff you would go through.

Now, all of my favorite players, with one exception, Bunny Berigan, were black. And I never liked any of the white bands. They had sort of a -- they didn't have any vitality, didn't have any -- well, I don't know what it was. You know, it was too wishy washy.
Well, I guess it wasn't original enough, or something, for you?

Well, you know, I've always judged music, books, painting, and people even, what happens to my heart. If my heart starts beating faster and your skin gets a chill and your hair sort of tingles, then you like it. And you could really distinguish between bands, then. You can't
Disciplined, man.
Yeah, basically it was cold, you know. They had nice chords and good soloists, but it was tight. You felt tight. And that would always, in those days, be the band that the white guys liked.

So I liked Jack Teagarden and I liked Benny Goodman, but my favorite trombone player was Lawrence Brown and my favorite clarinet player was Barney Bigard. And it once got me fired from Benny's band, for telling him that.

So all my favorites were that. And I'll tell you, it took me many years to get mad at a black guy, to be able to tell him to go screw himself, you know, because I was always sort of backing off. So in other words, I had a prejudice in reverse, there was a difference in my mind. It took me many years before I could behave the same to them as I did to anybody else. So in its own way, that was a prejudice.
Now, I don't know if I grew up with that or if I acquired it along the way but that doesn't matter. The point

is, I had it. Yeah, I'm sure. I've had that most of my life. I could remember working with guys like you, even as late as when we were down at Wister Hollow (PHONETIC), making all those dates. And of all my friends, all the guys that we were working with and yet, when you guys went to dinner, I always took off and would go some other place. Mainly because I didn't really know how to address myself to it and some places, I know, didn't want me in there. And they would perhaps be angry with you because you had brought me in there. And then rather than have it like that, I would go someplace else and meet you back there in the afternoon, for the dinner, for the next date. As late as that.
I'm ashamed that I never realized that. Because I have always been sensitive about that and sort of bend over backwards to be sure that doesn't happen.

Most guys were like that. I know my dearest friends like Buddy Laker and guys like that, we were together. But I would -- I can remember always (inaudible) I did because the inferiority was here and the inconvenience that that caused you. I didn't want anybody else to have to defend me. So I can understand your reverse prejudice.
Like when we were with Benny Goodman, joined the band. Well, I generally liked to room alone but we would get into a place like Ohio or someplace

and they wouldn't have any place for Cootie to stay. So I would check in in both our names and then Cootie would come in the room. And it broke my heart the first time he said, "You check in and I'll carry the bags in and act like I'm the band-boy." I said, "Bullshit. I'll check in and you walk in and I'll carry my own bags." That much I'll do.

So then he didn't want to go down to the dining room and he said, "We'll have room service." So I didn't want to go out and eat and leave him alone so it cost me a lot of money. But the first time I said, "Look, we'll go down to the dining room, you don't have to do anything. If they say anything at all, I'll pop them, you know." And he said, "No, I don't want to make any trouble and I don't want to embarrass you, embarrass the band. Leave it alone, it's all right."
So I know the feeling, that he just didn't want to put me on the spot.
Sure, it could be quite inconvenient and embarrassing on both sides.
But I've gotten into fights. During the war I remember I went on a bond drive down to Virginia. And Hernando, the Shakespearian actor, Hernando -- black actor, do you remember? (Juano HERNANDEZ)
Yes, I remember.
Hernando something, I can't think of his name right now. Well, he was a very interesting man to

talk to and we sort of palled around together and we played down in Norfolk, Virginia. And coming back, we're going back and we had a special coach on the train. And I was walking back to the Pullman with him and this cop standing by the gate says, you go through the other gate, to me. I thought, what the hell's the difference. I said, "I'm talking to my friend." He said, "This gate's for niggers, this gate's for whites!" And then I looked up, engraved in the marble, I mean for history to find, 2000 years from now they'll unearth this "Colored" "White". Gate leads right to the same platform, just a little piece of marble in between.

So I said, you know, told him to screw himself. And he called me a Negro lover and I went over and hit him. So all hell broke loose. You see, you hit a sheriff down South and you're dead. And the Pullman porter, of all guys, he was real stinky to me on the way down, very unfriendly. He came up to me running and said, "You dumb son of a bitch," and he grabbed me and ran into the train, he put me into an upper berth and closed me in. And then the cops came, you know, they were searching all over that train for me. And he said, "No, he took off down the street." I could hear voices out there.
So I have gotten into fights and I don't mind getting into fights about things. I don't think it does any good but sometimes it just makes me mad. But truthfully, I had this
incident, I don't know if you heard about it, when we were doing the Mildred Bailey Show. We had Charlie Shavers, Teddy Wilson, Al Hall, Specs Powell and Trummy Young.
What year was that?

1944. And Chesterfield -- '45. Chesterfield took the program over and they said -- not Chesterfield, Shube or somebody, the band leader or the advertising agency said, well, this is a Southern company, we can't have a mixed band for a Southern tobacco company. And we'll sneak them in later, in the back door.

So one day Teddy said -- Teddy and I used to be very good friends. And he said, "Are you going to do Chesterfield?" I said, "Sure, aren't you?" And he said, "No," and he got a funny look and he told me the story. So I called up the leader and said, "Look, I can't do it if my friends can't do it. I don't want to do it." And then I got thinking, Jesus, that's not really enough.

So I went up to the union, Willy Feinberg, he was a very militant guy, very leftist. Everybody was a little left then. And I told him the whole story and he got Schube down, Hailey, the guy from MCA who was Shriver, whoever was head of MCA. And he chewed them out. He said, "I'll take off every band off of CBS, I'll close every ballroom that uses an MCA band. You guys are out of work unless these guys start the show.
Well, I got threats to kill me, I got -- Martin Block wanted to bribe me $1,000.00. And, you know, even my friends said, 'You know, you're crazy. Your wife is pregnant and you sacrifice your career.'

The point that I'm trying to make is not that I was angry, and not because I was trying to fight a cause, it's just because it was my friends that they were hassling with, you know. I belong to the organizations like NAACP and Urban League and those things but I never thought too much of them, mainly because they were run by white people. And I didn't think anything would really happen until black people took over those organizations.

But in those days, you know, it was a white people's organization, they worked off their guilty conscience, whatever it was. They'd give money and sit down and have a cup of coffee with their maid and feel virtuous, you know.

I know you've always been so very liberal and kind and so helpful along all those causes. And your friends, I know you've had so many guys -- black friends, for example, I consider myself one, surely. And I can never forget your kindness to the late Ozie Johnson when he was ill. I remember one time you just called me off on the side and gave me $100.00 and said, would you please see Ozie gets this. I shall never forget all those kinds things you've done. And that has been consistent with your life.
I don't want to keep my mouth running but I did want to get back now to you, since you did mention when this has happened that your wife was pregnant. We haven't talked about your marriage.
Well, I guess the three most wonderful things in my life are my wife, my son and my daughter. And they came in fairly quick succession then.
I met my wife when I first joined Benny Goodman's band. Actually --
Her name?
Was Gertrude Bernstein and her brother was the bass player, Artie Bernstein, with Benny's band. And she came down to Atlantic City and I remember thinking, she's one beautiful girl.

Now, I had never seen many Jewish girls and I thought she was really an unusual kind of beauty. I thought she was the most beautiful woman I ever saw, you know. After seeing those washed-out blonds, you know. And this was a real thing. But I never did anything about it, you know. I had another girlfriend.

A year went by and we went to Catalina and she wanted to go into the ballroom one night and they wouldn't let her in. And jokingly I said, this is my wife and I took her in with me. So I don't know, I started kidding around and I said, 'Why don't you marry me.' Well, one thing led to

another. By the end of summer I was hopelessly in love with her and a year later I'd married her. And there was difficulty because her family didn't want her to marry a gentile and they didn't want her to marry a musician.
Two strikes, right there.

And Artie didn't want me to marry her for the same reason, plus the fact he was convinced I was a dope addict or something since I wasn't much of a drinker. And he was sure everybody did one or the other.
(Laughter.)

But everything turned out. Her elder brother, you know, pushed people through and we got married. And my son was born -- we were married in '41 and my son was born two or three years later. So that's -- no, he was born four years later, '45. So Gertrude traveled with the band for two years and then I decided I wanted to have a family. And my teacher, Benny Baker, he was a former first trumpet player with the NBC symphony, he said he could get me a job in the staff orchestra at CBS and for me to quit Benny's band and put my card in. So I did and went to work at CBS so I could have children. Because I didn't want to go on the road, you know, and have a family at home and everything. It's just no good.
And it was the surprise of my life when I left Benny's band. Benny had me so buffaloed I didn't think anybody would hire me. And within a week of quitting the band it seemed

like everybody in the country offered -- Basie offered me a job. And I said, why didn't you ever ask me before, for God's sake? And he said, "I couldn't afford to pay you." And I said, "you've offered me $100.00 a week more than Benny's playing me." He said, "I don't believe it." And I said, "That's right."
Woody Herman, everybody offered me jobs. But I determined to stay in town.
Your son was born in?
What's his name?
David, David Evans Maxwell. I gave him the middle name Evans after Gil Evans, who at that time was my best friend. Since then we've drifted apart quite a bit. But it's still a pretty name.

And my daughter was born three years after him and her name is Anne Reid Maxwell, after my grandmother, Anne Reid, my mother's mother. I don't know, in a burst of sentiment I did that. It was really unfair; I've thought about it over the years and I should have given her one of Gertrude's parents' names and one of my parents'. But in the Jewish religion, you don't name children after living people. And, see, we had to tell my mother-in-law that David was one of my relatives. David was just a name I liked from the Bible, King David, and I always liked that name. And said if I had a son, I would name him David.

The same thing came up when my son had his first son, he wanted to name him James Maxwell after me and his wife is Jewish and she wouldn't allow it. So he named him Justin, which is initial J, and gave him my father's first name, which is Kendrick, and it's also my middle name. Then recently he had another son, another baby, before she had it I said, "What are you going to name this one?" She said, "Well, if it's a girl, I'll name it James Maxwell." (Laughter.) So it was another boy.
You have two grandsons, huh?
Yeah, I have two and a half. I'll have a third one from my daughter in July. I hope she has a daughter, you know, then I'll have one of each. Or two of one -- have a set, anyhow.
Your son is a teacher, isn't he?

Yes, he teaches Russian at Tufts University. As a matter of fact, he's more or less the department head. I'm very proud of him, this year he won a large cash prize because he was voted the teacher of the year for Tufts University, both by the faculty and the student body.
What university is that?
Tufts.
Oh, yes. That's beautiful. I read some of these reports and I just wanted you to say it as a matter of record.

You know, it came -- when he graduated high school it was the summer I went to the Soviet Union with Benny Goodman, 1962. And I didn't really want to go and I was putting up all kinds of obstacles, asking a ridiculous price and then I said I wanted to take my wife, and Gertrude said she couldn't go and leave the children. So I said, well, I want to take my son. Benny said, 'Well, I'll give him a job in the band,' which later he didn't but I took him anyhow. Which was difficult, to take a member of the family to the Soviet Union. The state department of the Soviet Union's against it.

So I took him along with me and when he went to college he was going to be a chemist. And he thought about it and decided he wanted to study Russian because he wanted to go in the State Department. And he talked to the people in the Embassy in Moscow and he said, these people are hopeless, you know. They want war with the Soviet Union and everything else. He said, I feel I should do something for the government so I think I'll study Russian and go into the diplomatic service. But later he felt he'd rather be a scholar and he wound up going to the University of Moscow and he got his Doctor's degree and now he teaches at Tufts. So all from the trip with Benny Goodman.
That's beautiful. That's nice to hear.

That's how I met my wife, through Benny Goodman's band. My son picked his career through Benny Goodman's band. You know, with all the stories about Benny, I owe a great deal to him, really. He is a strange man but I always feel guilty when I say anything against him because I owe so much to him.

Well, I think music owes a lot to him. He's been very good to us through the ways in which -- black musicians. He was the first bandleader to make that giant step of putting them in his band, putting a black person in his band, which was Teddy Wilson, I believe. And I know, I've known him all my life since we were little kids. And I've worked for him and we've disagreed a million or more times. But just recently I had somebody ask me to name 10 people that I would put in a Hall of Fame and of course, I named Benny Goodman.

Yes. And of course, he stuck his neck out. You know, Benny is a very mercenary man, he's very interested in money. But he cut off almost half the country for that man. He didn't want to travel in the South with the band so he cut off a large part of his income. And I've heard him stand up, even in the New Yorker, the first time we went in there we had Sid Catlett, John Simmons, Charlie Christian, Cootie Williams, five or six black guys, I don't remember all. You know, you're working in a band, you forget who's black and
who's white. You know, you've got to start visualizing which is which. You see somebody enough, they don't have a color anymore.

And I remember the manager, I was standing there, saying, "I don't want these black guys coming in through the lobby and through the restaurant. In fact, I don't even want them here." And Benny said, "Well, I'm sorry. This is my band, if you don't want them in the band then screw yourself. We're walking out." So then he said, "Well, they'll have to go through the kitchen." Benny said, "They do not go through the kitchen." And then he said, "Well, all the musicians go through the kitchen." And Benny said, "None of the musicians go through the kitchen. They all come in the front door." "Well, then, they can't wear their uniforms when they come." Benny said, "Okay, all right, then they won't wear their uniforms."
(Laughter.)
(Inaudible).
But he stuck up for them. It wasn't just he put black guys in the band and then said, good luck, you know.
And it wasn't that he gave any particular race or guy a bad time. If he was giving anybody a bad time it was just he felt that way. It wasn't because of their ethnic background.
Yeah.
You mentioned that you studied Japanese. When did you take that up, Jimmy?

Well again, back to California. It's kind of a retroactive story. California had race laws against the Japanese. Japanese people could not own property, immigrants. So what they'd do, they'd get some friendly Caucasian to own the farm until their oldest son became of age and then they would buy it back in his name.

My grandfather owned a farm for this Takota family that lived next to us until Hijir --- Ijiro became of age. Ijiro was first son. Then he sold it to them for $1.00. So I used to play with the kids and picked up a little bit of the language. Then in 1936, in Los Angeles, I became very interested in Zen Buddhism and I met the Zen master from Japan and I learned more Japanese from him.

Then when the war started I was putting in my card at Columbia, at New York, I couldn't work for six months. So I went to Columbia and decided to learn to read and write it so I took 10, 12 semesters of it.
You Maxwells go in for exotic languages, and not the easy ones, man.
Well see, for me -- the point why I tell you all the background stuff, it wasn't all that exotic to me. It was familiar to me as Spanish was because I heard

a lot of Mexicans. I had a lot of Mexican friends and I knew a lot of Spanish, too. So, you know how it is in New York, like everybody knows some Jewish words, Italian words, and now they know Spanish words, I guess.
Sure. And then you studied Russian about the same time -- with your son or --

Well, when my son was a baby I used to take care of him every morning, get up with him and stay with him until noon. And, you know, playing with blocks and stuff like that isn't the greatest fun. So I would put on these Russian linguaphone records while I played with him. Maybe subconsciously he picked it up, too. And that's where I learned it.

Then when I went to the Soviet Union I took some lessons so I could talk it. But I've always been interested in communicating with people in any way, particularly in language. From the beginning, 1938, I first heard of semantics, the study of the emotional effect of words, you know, not just the dictionary meaning of words. I've always been interested in things about language, anyway. It's just interesting. I like to read grammars, I have about 30 languages at home. I like just to read -- I don't remember any of it, I don't learn the words, but just the words that they use, how they put them together is interesting to me. It's sort of like analyzing music, you know.
