You sure made great use of it. That's unique among musicians, I'll tell you that. These stories you're telling me are just most interesting.
Well, most musicians, I find, are pretty interested in languages. I know in Europe they've all got a smattering.
I speak Spanish with a Mississippi accent.
(Laughter.)

Well, that's what they tell me in France. Every summer I go to the same restuarant and the woman says, "You haven't learned French yet, have you?" And I said, "You understand me." She said, "Yeah, you speak very fluently and you have the worst accent and the worst grammar." And I said, "Well, do you understand me?" She said, "Yes." I said, "Well, then, why tire myself out trying to perfect it."

I did the same thing with Russian. I figure the Russians don't speak their own language all that good. They've got thousands of endings on words so I always mumbled the ending on the word and nobody ever gave me any trouble about it. In fact, one time a Russian soldier asked me some directions and I said I was sorry, I wasn't Russian, I was American and he wouldn't believe me. I was so elated.
(Inaudible).
Yeah, I thought, oh, boy, I did pretty good.

It's fun, you know, to go to a foreign country. You want to communicate with the people and I don't want to go there and just sit around and talk to the Americans all the time. And if you can say a few words, it just makes it more fun. You know, maybe I know two or three hundred words but I know how to put them together. That's the interesting part about languages, how to put the words together. And with two or three hundred words, you can say anything, actually. We don't use that many in English.
(Inaudible) few thousand words in our vocabulary.

We don't need them, you know. Good English is just clear thinking. It's not a fancy word, it's being able to think clearly and put it simply. That's good English, not big words. I think that would apply to any language. At least that's the principle I used.

Last Friday was St. Patrick's Day and I just happened to notice last Saturday. I just happened to notice, looking in the Musicians Union book in New York City, the only bagpipe player we have registered in the music book is James Maxwell. How'd you go about that, Jim?
Yeah. Well, you know, I told you my background. I don't think I can really claim to be pure

Scotch or Irish by any means but I've always loved the bagpipes. When I first came to New York, people asked me what I was, I'd say American. And that's not a good answer in New York, you know. In New York you've got to be an ethnic. So they'd say, "You've got a Scottish name, you must be Scottish. So I decided I'd be Scottish. Some of my ancestors did come from Scotland and I did hear a lot about it around the house, I heard some Scottish words, you know. I guess if there were any two outstanding cultures it would be Scotch and Irish.

But I would go to hear these pipe bands when they'd come to the Garden and tears would pour out of my eyes. So my wife bought me some pipes about 30 years ago and I went to a teacher and learned to play them. And it was kind of funny, in the beginning he gave me free lessons, he wouldn't take any money. And it came around January and he said, well, it's time to be measured up for the kilt. I said, I don't want a kilt, I just want to play the bagpipes. He said, well, you don't have to march in the parade but you can't do it without a kilt. I said I didn't plan on marching in the parade and he said, well, "Just because I gave you free lessons doesn't mean you're obliged to do it." I said, "Okay, Mr. Gallagher, okay." So I marched in the parade on St. Patrick's Day, walked right down by NBC and thought, Oh, God, I hope nobody comes out and sees me.
(Laughter.)
So for five or six years I marched in every St. Patrick's Day, I'd march in the parade.
Did you do it last Saturday?

No, last Saturday I was down in Florida. I haven't done it -- the band I was in sort of broke up about 10 years ago. And actually, I think the Sanitation Department took it over. They have a pipe band now and they wear the same kilt that we wore. And Mr. Gallagher retired to Las Vegas or some place.

He wound up traveling with the Kim Sisters, do you remember them? Three Korean girls that played all the instruments. And they decided they wanted to learn bagpipe, and they must have given him a fortune because he packed it in and went off with the Kim Sisters.
And he was an artist. God, he was a great piper.
I can't remember, one show I did or some band when --
Oh, I've done a lot of things, yeah.
Yeah, I remember being at some occasion where you played the bagpipes.

I've done a record with John Lennon and with this punk rock singer, what's her name? Patti Smith. On her last album. I generally just try to play traditional stuff but I've done an awful lot of jingles. They had one with Peter Sellers dressed as a Scotsman and that was me

playing the pipes. And they have another one for British Airlines showing a Scotsman over on a hill, it was me playing the pipes. I do a lot of jingles. Probably more jingles now on bagpipe than I do on trumpet. I'm pretty much out of that area. I do about two a year on trumpet.
And I'm not sorry, I don't miss it at all.
Not at this stage of the game. It's nice to sort of sit in the sun.
I don't need that much money now. I teach and play the kind of stuff I like to play. I'm back where I started, playing jazz again, and I'm the happiest I've ever been.
It's been a nice circle for us, you know.
Yeah, my style's coming back.

Sure, we started the hard way and made it through a very lucrative scene when the records were very popular, a lot of records were made. At the time we really needed it, when our children were growing up.
That's right. We were in on the start of television and tape.
Our careers have sort of paralleled along that line.
Half the dates I did were with you.
Sure. It's been a really nice thing
to see. Now as we settle down, all the young fellows have got to have a chance, we get back to playing a little jazz and teaching and doing some of the things we like to do.

I have 20 pupils so I have a good foundation with that. And they're getting better, thanks to people like Clark Terry and Jonah Jones, Doc Sevrinson. They send people to me all the time so I'm getting better pupils and whatnot. In fact, Jonah took some lessons from me, did you know that?
No, but I know you'd be good for him.

He gave me the most beautiful article in the Boston Globe, it was a half-page article. He had his teeth capped and he lost his lip. He couldn't make a single sound. I had worked out a system for things like that, or I had a guy shot up in the Korean War, how they can rediscover embouchure and build up a high register and everything. So I went -- I heard him practicing and he was just going (PANTING) for hours. And I asked him what happened and he showed me these big caps. And he used to have little stubby teeth and he couldn't get a sound. And he said, "I've got to open up at the Playboy Club in 10 days." So I said, "Well, I think I can help you if you want to work everyday."
And I thought, why the hell did I say that? I don't know. But I got in two or three hours everyday. And now here, I'm handling one of my idols, you know. And how are you going

to tell -- you sit there with a man you respect. And, you know, when he wanted to pay me I said, "Man, you've already paid me." He said, "What do you mean?" I said, "I practically made a career off Jonah Joins the Cab". I said, "half the things I play comes off your record, "Jonah Joins with Cab." I said, "You've paid me 1,000 times over." But he insisted on paying me. So by the end of ten days he had his lip back, he's playing up to high F. And he was in tears, you know. He said, "There are two people I love, I love Jesus Christ and Jim Maxwell and I don't know if that's the right order." And he gave this beautiful write-up to the Boston paper and told how I'd helped him.

Now, Buck Clayton had some trouble and he literally dragged him down to my studio and I gave Buck five or six lessons. And he wrote me a nice letter from Egypt and said it was just great. So I'm getting people like that.
Is he traveling now? Buck away?

Yeah, ever since he's been traveling. Because, you remember he had that concert in Paris when he got booed and he was crying. So Jonah said, "Well, look, I've been after you for six months." He said, "If you don't come down and see Jim, I'm going to drag you down."
Now, this other guy I used to stand down at the Apex Club on Central Avenue, listen to Buck, go home and try to remember what he'd played. How you going to charge a guy you

stole half your solos from, you know.

And to be a good teacher, you have to be an authority. Yet you've got men with -- you know, they don't have big egos in the sense that they're egotistical but they've got, you know, they're important people and they know they are. Now, you know, you can't treat them like a child. You've got to let that man keep his dignity but at the same time you do have to get in control. So it was the most ticklish thing I ever went through in my life.
(Break)
Well, just a little follow-up on that, you remember the time we went to Honolulu for that jazz festival?
: Yeah, sure.

Tommy was very impressed with my chops. He said, man -- you know, he kept raving about my range and endurance and my age and everything. And I told him about my system and everything and he said he had false teeth. And he said, would you come over and show me some day? I said, Tommy, you never sounded better. You don't need any help. You sound better than you ever sounded and better than anybody else." But he said, he taught and he wanted to find out about it and everything.

I didn't know how well it would work on a trombone because it involves being able to push the valves down with one hand while you hold the mouthpiece with the other. And it would be hard on the trombone to get different positions.
But he worked something out so we spent an afternoon together. And he wrote me a nice letter and said, you know, he really -- he does the system everyday. So I feel sort of proud about him.
He's a lovely man.

Oh, he's nice, he sure is. He was on that Mildred Bailey Show too, you know. He was always my favorite, next to Lawrence Brown. In fact, when we were in Honolulu I asked him, you know, I think, you know, like Trummy is the father of modern trombone playing in my opinion. Bill Harris and all these hotshot names and everything really got it from Trummy. And I used to get my head handed to me when I'd tell this to guys. "No, man." Et cetera.

So I told this to Trummy, I said, "How's it feel, you know, to have all these guys imitate you and everything?" He said, "I feel kind of complimented." I told him, "You know, you're really the father of modern trombone playing. I always believed Bill Harris copied you and everything." And I said, "I get my head handed to me for saying that." He said, "You know, that's true. Bill Harris told me so. He's a real nice guy and he always told me how much he appreciated, how much he'd gotten from me."
But I think that's true. That whole school of playing came out of Trummy Young.
That's very complimentary to say
that. What was that you were telling me about, an opposite story about what had happened to you before and what happened to you when you were with Redd Foxx?

Oh, yeah, going back to that story with the Chesterfield story and, you know, taking that case up to the union. While -- it reminds me of other stuff, too. First, while we were at the union these guys were saying, well, it's not that we're prejudiced against the black guys. But you know how it is, the black guy's a jazz musician, he can't read. And, you know, they're troublemakers. And Feinberg said, "Well, I've got a white, Anglo-Saxon man sitting here, Protestant -- he didn't know I'm not a protestant, who brought the charges up. The black guys did not bring the charges up, this white man did. So why don't you ask him about whether they can read." I said, "Well, Teddy Wilson is going to give a concert in Town Hall with Vera Landaska this week. Now, she's going to be very surprised to find out he can't read. And Charlie Shavers has played with this band and that band, first trumpet player." I said it was one of the most ridiculous accusations I had ever heard.

So repercussions went on through the years but the nicest one was 20 years later, I was playing at the Apollo Theater with Quincy Jones and Redd Foxx was the star, Billy Eckstine and Redd Foxx. And the last night -- well, Redd Foxx always kidded me, looked back and called me "The Lord," because
I had long hair. He said, "I knew everything was all right when I saw the Lord back there in the trumpet section."
(Laughter.)
And one morning Gertrude came in with me and he's sitting in the stage door and he says, "Morning, Jesus, Morning, Mary."
(Laughter.)

But it was that kind of thing. You know, just a joke back and forth. And the last night Jerome came down, Richardson, he was the contractor. He said, "Redd wants to see you up in his dressing room." I said, "Why?" And he said, "I don't know, I didn't ask him." So I went up. Redd said, sit down, have a drink, he gave me a drink. He said, "You know, I've been hearing about you from black musicians for years." And I said, "What do you mean?" He said, "That thing you did 20 years ago with the Chesterfield thing, with the radio program." And he said, "I always wanted to shake hands and say thank you. I read about it at the time." It was in the Amsterdam News. What was the name of that guy, he was a piano player, wrote a column for the Amsterdam News ?
: Dan Burley.

Dan Burley, yeah. He wrote a nice column about me. And he said he'd read it and he'd always heard about me and he wanted to meet me and shake my hand and thank me. And, you know, I'm very emotional. I started to cry. But
it was like it almost made it worthwhile, somebody thought I did -- I thought, Well, Jesus, once in a while I do something right in my life.

Well, you've done so many beautiful things. And Redd Foxx is a wonderful, powerful man. Throughout the whole black community we have such respect for him for when he finally made it and got to be a star, he went back and pulled out all the old entertainers. Just so beautiful.
Yeah, I know. Aunt Louise, is that her name? She used to be a snake dancer or something in some little club? He's got all his old buddies there.
He put them all out and (inaudible).
Well, black or white I think that's a great thing to do.
And most people seem to forget that but he found jobs for them. And he remembered the funny things they had done and got them in some spot where --

And he did. They're all great. The only thing wrong with that show is they got white writers because, you know, it's a white situation comedy with black actors. That was always a big disappointment to me. Black humor is so great, you know, that it's a pity that they don't have real black humor on there.
It has to be like jazz, it has to be improvised. A great deal of it has to be improvised and
Redd is really king of that.
Yeah, you know, he's great at what he's doing but he's a thousand times greater than that if they'd just let him go, you know.
Well, there were some good experiences, Jimmy.
Well, you know, you do a little here and a little there.
Quincy's band was up at the Apollo for a week.

A week or two weeks? Two weeks, the second time was two weeks. And that was right after the riots up there and Redd Foxx used to make the most outrageous remarks. He'd say, 'I saw you all on television. Hey, you out there with the greasy face, didn't I see you with a couple of hams under your arm?' (Laughter.) It's a wonder they didn't come up and kill him. And you know, the funny thing, I was getting the business from the guys on the 'Tonight Show.' Man, you go up there after the riots and everything, aren't you scared? I was never scared the whole time. Nobody bothered me, you know. I have never had trouble there, from the day I came to New York. People say, you're too big. But I think it's because I'm not frightened, you know.
That's the big part of it. There's
no criteria for it. But I feel the same way, Jimmy, and I know most of my friends, black friends, have had problems up there.

Well, I'm not frightened, I don't butt into what is none of my business. And if somebody looks me in the face, I look them in the eye and either say, good afternoon or I walk on and mind my own business. And nobody ever bothers me.
Now, you know, I'm not a fool enough to say that nothing could happen, because there are a lot of wierd people in the world. But I'm just saying nothing ever did. I'm probably lucky that way.
Thank heaven for that because you sure have done your share.
Yeah, one good pop and I'm out of business. Well, I would run. I'm not a hero.
Did you know Jack Jenny, know anything about him?

No, I didn't know very much about him at all. I have one or two of his records and I know his solos by heart, a couple beautiful tunes. And I knew the woman he was married to, Bonnie Lake I knew very well. She was a good friend of my brother-in-law's, Artie's. In fact, I still see her from time to time.
To wrap this up a little bit, can
you think of any tours or anything, some bands that might have given you a good laughs? When you went to Russia with Benny Goodman, you were on that first tour?

Yeah, that was pretty funny. You know, you don't like to tell tales out of school but I guess everybody knows that Zoot does take a drink once in a while and at that time, so did Phil Woods. And these guys were bombed from the start to the finish. And they drank the Russian wine and the Russians were sitting there looking at them like they're something from Mars, you know. But they secretly -- they did not like Benny, they hated him. They would spit when you mentioned his name because he gave them a hard time about sound and everything and they didn't feel like working that much so they didn't like him. But they all were fascinated.

And Zoot was taking photographs all through the Soviet Union and all of a sudden we realized nobody ever saw him put film in the camera. And Phil said, 'Man, what are you taking all those pictures for? You're so goddamned drunk you don't know where you are.' And Zoot said, 'That's why I'm taking them, man, when I get home I'll look at the pictures and know where I was.'
(Laughter.)
And Phil said, 'Yeah, but you never change the film, you keep doing the same one over and over.' Zoot said, 'Yeah, it's cheaper that way.'

When we were in Georgia, about the second place, we went to Tbilisi, it used to be called Tiflis (PHONETIC) in Georgia, and that's one of the Soviet Republics there. And we were riding on a bus going to the date every night and up in the front of the bus is a big sign in Russian. And Joe Wilder knew I could read Russian so Joe Wilder says, "What does that sign say?" I said, "Joe, I'm sorry you asked me that. You know where we are, Joe?" "Yeah, in Georgia." "It says, 'get in the back of the bus.'"
(Laughter.)

He says, "Oh, Jimmy, you dadblamed rascal." The president of Georgia had this big banquet for us and he said it was a Russian custom that he drinks 22 toasts in a row of big waterglasses of wine, everybody's got to empty them. And then he turns over the toast to somebody else. Well, that party is one of the funniest parties I ever went to because by the time everybody got through 22 glasses of wine, most people are pretty well bombed. And, you know, we had the CIA following us around, and newspaper reporters and people from Time and Life.

And so this Russian President of the Republic of Georgia gives a speech and the interpreter would say it in English. Then he'd say some more in Russian, then he'd say it in English and everything. And he gets through with his 22nd toast so he turns it over to Benny Goodman. And Benny

gets up and he starts to make a speech and the interpreter speaks in Russian and it's translated in English. This is funny, also. Benny goes into this long story about how he worked all his life. And he says, "A few years back a woman came into my life that changed everything." And his wife's with him and his two daughters, a stepdaughter and real daughter, and they're both preening, you know, wondering which one it's going to be. He says, "This woman has meant more to me and done for me," and goes on and on and they're wondering, is it going to be Alice or Angie, whatever his daughter was.
And he said, "I'd like to propose a toast to Muriel Zuckerman."
(Laughter.)

Shortly after that Alice went back to the United States. By this time, though, everyone's pretty well gone. Phil Woods stands up and says, "I'd like to make a speech." And he gets -- the alto player, Jerry Dodgion, he says, "Translate, motherfucker." So Jerry Dodgion goes (Unintelligible). So Phil goes on and he's harranguing and he says, "translate, Motherfucker." And then Phil starts talking double talk and the guy from the Embassy's trying to pull him down. And Phil says, "All right, you don't want me to talk." And everyone's looking at him, he sits down and two gallons of wine come out all over the table. And everybody's shocked and upset and they're saying, what an impression Americans are making on
on the Russians. I told them, boy, you know, anyone who drinks 32 toasts in a row has seen a drunk before. I said, don't worry about it.

So we go back to the hotel on this bus and one of the interpreters, this girl is sitting with me. And both Phil Woods and the trombone player, he used to be married to a French horn player, black girl who was a French horn player.
Wayne Andre.

Wayne Andre, they're both hitting on this girl. She's sitting on my lap and there's some Georgian, I think he's a little sweet, was trying to hit on me, and it was a real complicated situation. She's sitting on my lap because there's no other room for her to sit. And David was sitting next to me.

We get to the hotel and Phil and Wayne get into an argument and Phil starts with the 'motherfucker.' And Wayne says, 'Just a minute, you son of a bitch, you can't speak like this in front of a fucking lady,' or something. In front of the Russian girl, you know. And these girls are pretty tough, they say they're KGB or whatever, you know. They're not shocked by anything. And they're going to square off and have a fight.
And this I don't think is good for the American image. So I picked Phil Woods over my shoulder, put him over my shoulder and carried him up three flights of stairs. And

he's screaming and kicking me. So I got him up in the room and I said, "Shut up, you son of a bitch." So I pulled his pants down and put him over my knee and whipped him with a hairbrush. And everyone's wondering, where is Zoot. I opened the door, here's Zoot like an angel, lying in bed. What's all the fuss, you know?

So then guys are -- the whole trip was like that. It's just one thing after another. The only thing that was fairly calm was the 4th of July. We were invited to the Embassy for the 4th of July party and that morning all of the Russians very seriously came up and shook my hand to say congratulations on the anniversary of your revolution. I said, "That's right, it was a revolution."

And I see a crowd of people and Benny says, "Come over here." I came over and there's a little fat guy standing there. Benny says, "Meet Premier Krushchev." So I pull out my Russian and say (RUSSIAN), "I'm glad to meet you." And Krushchev said, in Russian, you speak very good Russian. Then he said something I couldn't understand and everybody laughed. He said, "You're the only American he's ever been afraid of." I said, "Why?" He says, "Bolshoi". I just towered over him, he came below my belly. He said I was the only American he was ever afraid of.
That American image is quite cheesy(?) in Moscow, isn't it?

Well, that was in the missile crisis. We were in Tashkent when they had an air raid drill right in the middle of the Cuban missile crisis. And Dave and I were up in our hotel room looking out on the balcony and these soldiers come running up in our room with these Kelishnokov automatic rifles, or something, and scared the Jesus out of me. They drag us into the room, pull the blinds, yell at us in Russian, go through all our drawers and then run back down the street. So we turned out the lights and peeked out and they're sitting up antiaircraft guns out on the square out in front. I thought, "Oh, God, Kennedy's really blown it while we're gone. This is it." That was one of the scariest nights I ever had.
That's quite of a big country, isn't it.
It's enormous.
I couldn't really see being so big.

Well, we flew -- the last trip I made in '73, whenever it was, with the George Wein's company with the tribute to Louis Armstrong, we flew from Moscow to Siberia, which is about one-third of the way across the country and which is as far as it was from Moscow to the United States, you know. God, took us something like ten hours to get there.
One city from Moscow, it would be like going from New York to California instead of like New York
to Chicago.

Oh, just a short distance up to Leningrad is a five or six hour flight. It's like going to California. Yes, it's an enormous country, all right. I liked both trips there. It was very interesting and I'm glad I went.
That's one of the nice things about being a musician, isn't it?
Oh, yeah.
We've really had some opportunities to see the world.

Yeah. Well, you know, I grew up looking at National Geographics, and things and dreaming. You know, you live in the middle of a desert, your father's out of work for four years, you don't think you're ever going to even get out of Tracy, little loan to these glamorous places like that. And the last few years, you know, I've been going to Nice every summer. And I don't do anything else, I've done more than I ever thought I would.

That's right, I feel the same way. I mean, being born in Mississippi, being black, I never in my wildest dreams have dreamed -- and yet, I thought that we were poor by the standards of America, blacks in Mississippi in 1910 when I was born, we were really poor. But man, I've been in some countries of the world where we, by their standards, were
really well off.

Yeah, that's what Budd Johnson was saying. The last time we were in the Soviet Union, Bud was there. And we were in a foreigners dining room and some African revolutionaries came up. They had outfits and everything and gave the Communist salute and started calling him "Brother" and how did he like it when he was in the land of freedom, and so forth. Budd looked at them and said, "Man, I would rather be back in Mississippi starving."
That's right, really.
He said, "You've got to be kidding."

I was thinking, I was taking my wife to a little vacation in Jamaica and I saved all the money I'd made at RCA and Columbia/ I've got a pocket full of money and I'm going to a black country and just really groove. And when I saw the poverty of the people, I cried. I'm staying at a hotel paying $67.00 a day, and I walk out and see a little old lady that looked like my grandmother would probably have looked, with 12 layers in front of her in that hot, 120 degree sun. It really gives you some perspective about where we live in comparison to the rest of the world.

You said it made you cry. You know, so many Americans many years back liked to go to Spain. They said, oh, it's cheap to live in Spain or it's cheap to go to the islands. I'd say, "Did you ever look around and see why

it's cheap to live there? You know, you can get help for 50 cents a day, why do you think you can get help for 50? Because they're starving to death, doesn't that bother you?" "No, no, man, that's the way things are."

I see another black man there, he's got a palatial place and three cars, and he's got a black boy working for him, he's paying him 75 cents a week. He's got -- he's climbing trees to get his food, get the coconuts down. And I said, "How can you treat a kid like this, you're not even sending him to school. He's the same color as you."
That's what convinces me that we're all human beings, we're all alike.
Yeah. He said, "You don't understand." I said, "Okay, I don't want to."
Yeah, I believe the skin makes no difference underneath. Because underneath you're going to find the same bastard or the same saint. It has nothing to do with what's underneath.

Well, you know, you go back to this business about slavery. Who the hell sold them the slaves in the first place? The black chieftans would sell slaves, the Arab traders. The only slavery country today is in Africa. Then later the Americans and English would go raid and cut out the middleman, but in the beginning they were selling their own people.
Selling their own people, kidnapping
I tell you, it sure gives us a great perspective, as musicians, because most of us have come from ordinary backgrounds, none of us have --
Oh, yeah, very few musicians come from rich backgrounds.
And it's given us a chance. And to be able to travel when you're sort of -- you know, when you can look at it in this perspective.
You know, I think we'll just knock it off for now. It's been so beautiful I don't want to tire you.
(End of Reel 1, as recorded.)

Interview with Jimmy Maxwell
Reel 2
Conducted by Milt Hinton
April 16, 1979

This is Monday, April 14th, right?
No. 16th. Friday the 13th, I remember, so it's 14, 15, 16. Friday was the 13th.

Yeah. This is a continuation of that great session we were having talking with you. That's a beautiful story you were talking about there. And I just happened to mention to you in our conversation while we were setting up the tapes about some situations I'm sure you've been involved in and you've seen.

First, I'd just like to say that my conception of one of the reasons you are so much necessary for these archives is because of your great contribution to music and to jazz and your involvement, socially, with so many musicians of all colors and races. You're interested in languages, you're interested in people, and this kind of musician is certainly -- his records will certainly be read by future musicians, what it was like to be a musician and how it come about. Because sometimes we have to follow, we are what proceeded us in most cases. We build on our ancestors, our habit forming, our training. We may deviate and go in one special direction, but we are certainly influenced by them.
And I just happened to mention I have difficulty sometimes describing to young black musicians who don't know too much about their background, the younger ones nowadays, in the

seventies, doesn't seem too much interested. And I made the statement that now that so many of our greats have passed like Louis Armstrong and Charlie Shavers and Jelly Roll Morton and any number of greats, Jimmy Blanton, that many young blacks don't really know anything about them or even be too interested in learning.
And you made a statement to me about what you thought when you have run into that. Please, go on now.

Well, it came about I had written -- transcribed some arrangements for Mercer Ellington that had been lost after Duke's death. And one was on "Congo Brava" and Ben Webster made a classic tenor solo that was famous with most musicians. And I had just written in the chord symbols, I didn't write it out. And a friend of mine, Dave Burger (PHONETIC), had copied the arrangements, and Harold Ashby, who's a great tenor sax player and a great friend of Ben Webster's, was going to play the solo.

And then Dave said to him, well, Jimmy didn't transcribe Ben's solo, but I guess you know it if you want to play it. And Ashby said, I think he was serious, says, "I don't know anything about that solo." And Dave and I looked at him, sort of in amazement. I said, 'how come you don't know it?' And then in other incidents, the fact that you don't find young -- you know, you don't see young black musicians playing like Louis, or anything.

I thought about it a great deal and the explanation seemed to me, and I think it's likely, the young black musician is not interested historically that -- he doesn't have the time, he doesn't have the money. Most musicians, black or white, I think, come from poorer circumstances. But the historical aspect of music and jazz is a hobby that takes money to follow. And the young black musician coming up is interested in playing like contemporary musicians that are successful, because he's got a very pressing problem, which is to make a living. And he doesn't have the time or the money to indulge in a hobby like history.
(Break)

At least, I think this has been true all along. I know even in my own case, it was easy for me to think that way because when I was young, my father was in the Depression, we had no money, and it was enough for me to keep up with the records that came out once a month, Louis Armstrong or Duke Ellington, which in my day was the modern, radical music. But I knew nothing about Louis Armstrong and the Hot Five, I couldn't have afforded to go back and buy all those records, myself. Now, I think the same situation applies to the young musicians today, particularly the black musicians who have the pressing necessity of making money.
Now again, the white musicians had much more chance of making money because the work by cotell (PHONETIC) bands and that kind of thing where they could make a living, not
playing music they particularly liked, gave them a chance to make enough money to investigate and to backtrack and to look into the past.

So I don't think it's indifference on the part of the young black musician, but I think it's economic pressure. He just doesn't have the time and he's too involved trying to make a living and trying to keep up with the contemporary style, which is quite a bit to keep up with because it's so technical. You know, he'd have to spend his whole time practicing now.

Yeah, right. Thank you for your great defense. I think that's good. We're sitting on opposite sides of the fence and I'm on the side you're talking about, only as a senior citizen now. But I'm concerned with -- I've listened to Prez, when he was living, talk about how he was influenced by some great white players like the great saxophone player that was with Paul Whiteman's band that played C melody saxophone.
Yeah, I keep thinking Teschma ker
It wasn't Teschma ker. It was the guy who recorded with Bix Beiderbecke all the time.
Yeah, I can't recall his name right now.
It's terrible, I can't think of his name, either.
Might be Trumba er.
Trumbauer yeah.
I have known Trumbauer what an excellent musician he was, and he really did, if you think about it --

Oh, yeah, I do believe it, yes. I do believe that. And I like Trumbauer myself. That's one of the few musicians from that circle -- I never liked Bix Beiderbecke. I never understood what the hollering was all about. And the funny thing, the first person that made me see any value at all, was Lloyd Reese, a black trumpet player. And he said, don't put him down just because he doesn't sound like Louis Armstrong. He said, there's a lot to learn from him. And he pointed it out but at that time I couldn't see it. Now, of course, I can see some value. But I still can't say truthfully -- that impresses me.

Yet, to take the opposite side of what you say of events, I agree with you on events, the young black player, perhaps, he might be crowded. But now that we have schools and quite a number of our young black musicians are in school, and we have jazz workshops, we have some people -- we're beginning to get into that. But I find that some of our regular -- some of our popular black stars are not -- don't go back and do a Louis Armstrong song in 1979. I happen to remember hearing some black instrumentalist that had recently done something on shades of Bix. I haven't heard anybody doing

anything on Shades of Louis, some name players. You know, I don't want to throw anyone's name in particular, but I was wondering -- and yet we have some white players that have been doing some excellent jobs on recreating and reviving and bringing a rebirth to some of our great black composers, like Jelly Roll and some of great pianists. We know who they are. And I don't remember, recently, any of our name black artists doing this kind of thing. I was wondering what you think about that?

I think that you can't criticize the black teachers any more than you criticize white teachers, because all teachers nowadays, black or white in any subject, seem to be more interested in conducting a popularity contest with the young people rather than trying to direct them, which a teacher should be doing. Rather than trying to present them with something at first they may not want to know and then showing them the value of it, I think -- I'm talking about all teachers. My son is a teacher and I hear many stories about this anxiety to be popular with the pupils. And I think perhaps they resist doing that because they don't want to present something to the pupils that's going to cause a struggle at first. And I think that could be one explanation.
Because I know that the pupils -- and you know, if you talk about Louis Armstrong right away they say, oh, yeah, I know him, 'Hello, Dolly,' you know. And they don't know
anything about the dynamite stuff he did in the 20's and 30's.
You know, there's some talk in some circles, him being an Uncle Tom, from people who have no relativity with the era in which Louis lived. And how he had to survive.

Well, he survived. And if it wasn't for him, you wouldn't have the young people today who are in a position where they can call him an Uncle Tom, and get away with it. He made his little remarks. You know that yourself, like he'd make his little digs on records, like "Just a Gigolo," he slips in, "when I die I know they'll say, just another jig." And here and there, "shine," "chocolate drop, that's me" and sang it with great feeling. And although, "Black and Blue," "What did I do to be so black and blue," wasn't his song, and he didn't change the words, he sang it with sincerity. I think there was no mistaking that song was written for him. And it could make a white person feel black when you'd hear it, if it's possible. I could have cried right along with him when he did that record.
I know, I've felt that same thing.

So I don't think he has to apologize to anybody or anybody has to apologize for him. It's shocking that a lot of people who said that were musicians themselves, and were angry young musicians at the time. But you know, going back to black musicians doing it, you take guys like

Clark Terry, Dizzy Gillespie, Ernie Royal, who were older than those other two, they know a lot of Louis's stuff, much to my surprise. And they're considerably younger, you know. They weren't learning at the time that Louis was at his peak. Well, Dizzy is not ten or fifteen years younger, he's the same age as me. But Clark is younger and a lot of good musicians know it.

But see, I think also then when a black musician gets good and he gets his own style going, he becomes creative, he doesn't listen any more anyhow, because he's got his own thing going now, his own creativity and --

Well, I can understand that because music is very jealous. In order for one to create, one can't spend too much time listening to something else because it might detract, it might detract from what you're doing.

It's very dangerous. You know, in the beginning you have to -- just like a child has to learn to speak by copying his mother and father's speech patterns, but at a certain point, much to the parent's disappointment, the child starts speaking for himself. And I think a good jazz player has to do that. And I can speak from experience that sometimes you can hang on to your mother's apron strings too long.

I mean, some of these guys, conservatory musicians talk about jazz players, they ought to practice one-half as hard and one-half as intelligently or as musically as these guys. That's right, d-r-y, l-o-n-g, s-o.
Okay, that's what I thought. I heard --
you know, I remember that from 1933, and I have never heard anybody say it.

Well, you know, because so many black people are uneducated they would have a natural genius for language. They would have been Shakespeare, maybe. So it came out in some of these godawful expressions, the most beautiful expressions you can ever think of. In a way you almost say, I hope they never get educated because --
So descriptive.
Some of the creations were so great.

So very descriptive. I know the great black jazz poet, John Hendricks, he has some tremendous expressions like that. He compares a West Indian black and a Caribbean black to an American black in a song which he sings, 'If you have a ship and you needed some rum, then you would stop at the Islands. So some stopped on the way to trade some slaves for some rum,' and he says, some stopped on the way, and the rest came on to the U.S.A. And he says, the ones in the U.S.A, they had to use a new language, so they got as close as they

Well, so does any European, because most people in the world don't have the th sound. They say Tee in their language where we say th. So when they try to say th they say tat, or Germans say dat, because that's the way they say it. So blacks are not the only ones. There are only two languages in the world, English and Icelandic, I think, that say th. So the rest of the word says tis and tat.
It's interesting to observe these --

Well, that's something that always interested me. You know, many black people don't know the meaning of that song, "Strutting With Some Barbeque," but that was a West Coast expression for a good looking girl, barbeque. Another tune he wrote was called "Beaucoup Jack".
"Beaucoup Jack."
Yeah, well, that's right. Some French people were saying, what does that mean. I said, well, you ought to know, of all people. Jack means money, beaucoup --
A lot of money, beaucoup Jack, that's right.
That's a New Orleans -- it must have been a Creole expression for a lot of money, yeah.

Oh, yeah, that's strictly French.

Creole French. She would tell me to go to the store and get a dime's worth of lanyet and a nickel's worth of sweet potatoes in Mississippi. And she says, Turn the lanyet me an onion. Now, if one of my neighbors sent me to the store, she would have to give me the lanyet for going, so I could lanyet up a piece of candy. (Laughter.) She had many more, just beautiful. That's what's so remarkable about you, Jimmy, you've come through these different things and not only have you made a study of languages but you've made a study of people and been involved with so many different people and different ethnic backgrounds, and you've been able to survive and make friends with them.

really know what, ethnically, I am. But I've had Italians say, you act like you're Italian, or I was in the Soviet Union, "Are you sure you're not Russian?" So I'm about as close as you can get.
Sure everybody feels that way.
I don't know whether I'm a chameleon or what I am.

You're a chameleon soul. Like you came in here the other day, walking through the kitchen, and my wife had some cornbread up there, and you jumped right in just like you were a brother and really enjoyed a slice of it.
Well, I grew up on that stuff. That was good, though.
We weren't going to offer any to you because we didn't want to scratch your throat.
(Laughter.)
What do you think we ought to talk about now? Let's hold it a while.
All right, pull ourselves together.
We were talking, Jimmy, about your teaching. I know you were talking about these young people who come to you and some of them are very anxious, because I have that same

problem, some young people come to me and say, 'look, I want you to teach me a song.' I say, well, I'm not going to teach you a song, I'll teach you to play conserva-tive bass and you conservative trumpet. And you mentioned how you have to straighten them out.

And I also know that you've been able to straighten out and help some of our really, truly great professional guys who really love you, and know how you really have the sympathy to want to help them. And I was just telling your story about Jonah Jones with he was in Cuba and he had a little trouble in Cuba because he drank the wrong kind of beer that paralyzed his chops and he got sick once and I know he came to you. What was that about?

Well, he didn't really come to me. I used to practice up in the studio, up next to his, and he'd come in there occasionally, up at Colin's Practice Studios. And one time I was teaching up there and I heard somebody in the next room, and I hear this huff, huff, for about an hour, and I thought maybe this was some new system. And I went in and asked Charlie, who's in there. And he said, 'Jonah Jones, he's lost his lip.' And I said, oh, my God, and I stuck my head in and said, hello, what happened?

He said, well, I got my teeth capped, because he used to grind his teeth and his teeth were down almost to the gums. And the dentist gave him these big, beautiful teeth, without taking into consideration he was a trumpet player, and Jonah

just couldn't get a sound. And he said he opened up in the Playboy Club in Chicago in 10 days and he didn't know what he was going to do. I said, it looks like you're going to have to stand around and smile a lot, because that's all you've got going, sort of kidding.

And then I said, you know, I have this sort of system, it was to help a kid that had braces on their teeth, and then I found out it was very good for developing a register and things, basically it's trying to develop a new embouchure because, you know, a person's been playing a certain length of time and they've got a lot of strength, they don't progress, obviously they don't have the right setting on their mouth, then. And I had discovered a way to get around what holds you back from developing. And I said, I think I can help you. He said, gee, that would be great. And I said, if you've only got 10 days, we'll have to get together everyday for the 10 days. Great. I said, well, as soon as this lesson's over -- so I sat there and I said, why did I open my big mouth, I don't know whether I can help him or not.

But I was very enthusiastic about this system, I still am, actually. So we went in, and the big problem. Here's an established musician that I admired, and you know, I had practically made a career out of "Jonah Joins Cab," that record, took a lot of good stuff off that record. You know, I had heard him with Stuff Smith and in '36 I heard

him out at a Famous Door in Hollywood. It was the first time I hever heard a guy play four or five chords in a row, he used to play "Stomping at the Savoy" and end up on a high A-flat. Shake the room, this big, fat sound. He's always been one of my big idols, he's great. And I felt sorry for him.

So the problem is, you know, to be an effective teacher, you have to be in charge, and the pupil has to have faith in you. But, you know, you can't come on strong with this guy who was a great artist, you know, it's not the same as somebody else, you have to let him keep some of his dignity, yet you have to get control. And it's one of the most ticklish things I ever went through, I would be exhausted. And we worked together for an hour, two hours everyday.

And Jonah was great, you know, he was very relaxed, and he would go very carefully. It took me about two and a half hours with him because he would tell a few stories and talk. And, you know, the main thing was to get him -- he was terrified, you know. I don't blame him, of course he's terrified. Well, by the end of the 10 days he was up to high F's and high G's and he was really happy. And I had given him all these different exercises. And I said, you've got to call me up from Chicago. He called me up the first night and said, I don't know how to thank you. He said, it's just gone great.
About two weeks later he said, you know, I've got a problem. On the second set I'm getting very tired. I said,

Well, you know, maybe we'll cut down. Are you doing the routine I gave you? And he said, yes. I said, well, what are you doing? I had given him three or four different routines to practice at separate times. He was doing the whole damn thing everyday. I said, good, God, how do you play the first set? You're only supposed to play one-third that much. So we set it out.
Now, when he went to Chicago he had a big interview with the newspaper up there which I got a copy of. He must have spent three columns telling, you know, what I'd done for him and everything.
That's beautiful, that's so nice to hear.
And he told my wife once, he said there's two people in the world I respect, Jesus Christ and Jim Maxwell. And I don't know if that's the right order.
That's beautiful.

He kept coming back. And then everytime he'd be in town he'd come for some more lessons. And I didn't want to charge him. I said, how can I charge this man. I told Jonah, I owe you so much, there's so much I got from you, I can't charge you, for God's sake.
I'm sure he's grateful.
He was very --he flatly refused and I had to charge him by the hour, not by the lesson. I said, well,
I get $25.00 a lesson. He said, well, some of those lessons are three hours, you ought to get double for those. I said, no, it's just for a lesson. And needless to say, he paid me more than I wanted.

Then about a year later he said, 'would you do the same for Buck Clayton?' I said, well, I'd heard about Buck and I wanted to offer, I sent word to Buck that maybe I could help him. But, I said, it's the same kind of situation, I've known him and he knows me, and it's hard to have any faith in somebody that you've seen around, you know. Well, you know, the young players should memorize everything the can. Now, not everybody can memorize, it's not easy. But there's a very lucky thing, there's an awful lot of solos transcribed now. And I know with my pupils, I give them a solo every week or every two weeks, of some famous solo, and I make them learn it like an etude. I say, don't come in here and bluff your way through it, learn that like you're practicing Arvins or ____, I don't give a damn. You learn that like an etude and I don't want you to come in here and try to sound like Freddie Hubbard or anybody else, sound like you, you know. I want you to take this solo and make it you not him. Because you're never going to play like that. Come in and play it your way because these are just notes. Forget what he sounds like.
And then I make them learn their chords on that solo, be able to play all the chords from that solo and all the scales associated with those chords. And then we pick another

solo.
Now, I think that's a good thing to do, even if you do copy solos. It's one thing to be able to sing along with a soloist, another thing to get it with your fingers. And you've got to practice to get it in your fingers. And I'm surprised, most people don't know how to practice. You know, you don't just make a mistake and go back and play three notes, oh, there it is, then you go ahead. If you make a mistake, I don't care if you had it perfect all week, you go back and you practice with a metronome, you set it at half the speed and move it up one notch at a time. And generally it comes out to about 20 times, until you get it up to the speed it should be. Then you go and play it through.
Now, if you make that mistake again, you do the same process. You don't say, oh, I know it, I just made a mistake. You never say, oh, I know it, I just made a mistake. And so if you do that, then you're going to have it in your fingers. Otherwise you've got what you call a b.s., a bullshit technique, you know. One time you can do it, another time you can't. But when you take it from half speed to full speed, you get control of your muscles. So your muscles respond to your mind and you improve your chances of getting it right, 100 percent.
So I think, these books are all over the place, they're published illegally and legally. There's a book of Charlie Parker's solos, something like 40 solos in there, literally, 40 solos,
